name: Camera angle / eye dominance selection
lead: Camera angle and eye dominance selection is the practice of choosing which side of the face, and which angle, to present to a camera, sometimes with reference to a person's dominant eye. The idea is that most faces look better from one side than the other.

Research on facial symmetry reports that faces are not perfectly symmetric: on average the eyes, nose and mouth sit slightly to the left relative to the ears, so the right side of the face appears larger.[1] Symmetry increases attractiveness ratings, more so for female faces.[1] Wikipedia's facial symmetry article does not state that either side is preferred.[1]

Ocular dominance is the tendency to prefer visual input from one eye; about 70% of people are right-eye dominant and 29% left-eye dominant, and it is mainly studied for aiming tasks.[2] No source reviewed links eye dominance to choosing a flattering camera side.
infobox: Evidence for eye dominance and flattering side

paras: The face is systematically offset: the eyes, nose and mouth are on average slightly left relative to the ears. This aurofacial asymmetry is about 2 degrees at birth and about 0.5 degrees in adults. During speech, 76% of people show greater mouth movement on the right side.[1]
Researchers caution that mirroring one half of a face to create a symmetric image can produce artificial features, such as an oversized or undersized nose.[1]

Eye dominance is only loosely analogous to handedness, and the dominant eye and dominant hand often differ. It can shift with gaze direction, task and fatigue. Tests include the Miles and Porta tests, the Dolman method and lens fogging.[2] The article notes that dominance matters for aiming sports and monovision contact lenses, and that fMRI shows brain activity differences in face perception by dominance, which concern how faces are processed and not how they look.[2]
A 2013 study in the journal Laterality asked whether the advent of the camera changed the side of the face that artists chose to show in self-portraits.[3]
No studies found on choosing a camera side by eye dominance. Related research on facial asymmetry, attractiveness and portrait orientation exists.[1][3]

card.summary: Picking a 'better side' for photos; faces are measurably asymmetric, but no source links eye dominance to a flattering angle.
card.note: Research covers general facial asymmetry; eye dominance as a selection rule is untested.

quick.overview:
Many people photograph from a preferred side of the face, and some tie that choice to eye dominance.

Faces are known to be slightly asymmetric on average, but the sources reviewed do not say either side is preferred, and none links eye dominance to a flattering angle.
quick.mechanism: People pick the side or angle they judge as more symmetric or flattering. Eye dominance is the preference for one eye's visual input, about 70% right-dominant.
quick.risks: No physical risks. The practice is untested for effect on perceived attractiveness.
